term: Derivation of the conjugate gradient method
definition: In numerical linear algebra, the conjugate gradient method is an iterative method for numerically solving the linear system A x = b {\displaystyle {\boldsymbol {Ax}}={\boldsymbol {b}}} where A {\displaystyle {\boldsymbol {A}}} is symmetric positive-definite, without computing A − 1 {\displaystyle {\boldsymbol {A}}^{-1}} explicitly.
details: The conjugate gradient method can be derived from several different perspectives, including specialization of the conjugate direction method for optimization, and variation of the Arnoldi/Lanczos iteration for eigenvalue problems. The intent of this article is to document the important steps in these derivations.

explainer.lead: This derivation explains how the conjugate gradient method obtains its search directions and step sizes for solving Ax=b. It matters because the method can solve a symmetric positive-definite system iteratively, using A directly rather than explicitly forming its inverse.

tiers.eli5: Imagine trying to reach the bottom of a smooth valley while carrying a set of directions that do not undo your earlier progress. Conjugate gradient chooses such directions, decides how far to travel along each one, and stops when the remaining error is small enough.
tiers.practitioner: Use it for symmetric positive-definite linear systems, supplying matrix–vector products with A, a right-hand side b, an initial guess, and a stopping tolerance. Check symmetry and positive-definiteness, monitor the residual, and remember that floating-point rounding can disturb the ideal direction relationships.
tiers.paperLevel: Given symmetric positive-definite A and Ax=b, define r_k=b-Ax_k and minimize the quadratic objective f(x)=1/2 x^T A x-b^T x along A-conjugate search directions. The updates are alpha_k=(r_k^T r_k)/(p_k^T A p_k), x_{k+1}=x_k+alpha_k p_k, r_{k+1}=r_k-alpha_k A p_k, beta_k=(r_{k+1}^T r_{k+1})/(r_k^T r_k), and p_{k+1}=r_{k+1}+beta_k p_k. The method can be derived by specializing conjugate-direction optimization or by varying the Arnoldi/Lanczos iteration, and its standard form requires A to be symmetric positive-definite.

explainer.example: For A=[[2,0],[0,1]], b=[2,1], and x0=[0,0], start with r0=p0=[2,1]. The first step gives alpha=5/9 and x1=[10/9,5/9]; the next conjugate-direction step gives x2=[1,1], which satisfies Ax=b exactly.

explainer.goal: Derive and carry out iterative updates that approximate the solution of Ax=b without explicitly computing A inverse.
steps: Update x=x+alpha p and r=r-alpha A p.
Stop if the residual is sufficiently small.
Otherwise set beta=(r_new^T r_new)/(r_old^T r_old), form p=r_new+beta p, and repeat.
tradeoffs: Standard derivation requires symmetric positive-definite A
Rounding can affect ideal residual and direction properties
